title: Files & JSON
summary: Read and write text files safely, then load and save structured data with JSON — the format that powers APIs and AI tools.
objectives: Open, read, and write text files using Python
Use the with statement so files always close safely
Choose the right file mode: read, write, and append
Understand what JSON is and why it powers APIs
Convert between Python objects and JSON strings
Load JSON from a file and save Python data back to JSON

quiz.q: What does the with statement give you when opening a file?
options: It closes the file automatically when the block ends
It converts the file to JSON
quiz.why: with open(...) as f: guarantees the file is closed even if an error happens, so you never leak open file handles.

quiz.q: Which file mode overwrites an existing file from scratch?
quiz.why: "w" (write) truncates the file to empty before writing. "a" appends to the end; "r" only reads.

quiz.q: Which Python function turns a Python object into a JSON string?
quiz.why: json.dumps serialises (dumps) an object to a string. json.loads does the reverse. The s stands for string.

quiz.q: What Python type does a JSON object become when you load it?
quiz.why: A JSON object with key/value pairs maps directly to a Python dict; a JSON array becomes a list.

quiz.q: Why must you specify encoding="utf-8" when opening files?
quiz.answer: So accented and non-English characters are read and written correctly across systems.
quiz.why: Without an explicit encoding Python uses the OS default, which can corrupt characters like é or — on Windows.

quiz.q: What is the difference between json.dumps and json.dump?
quiz.answer: dumps returns a JSON string; dump writes JSON straight to an open file.
quiz.why: Same for load (reads from a file) versus loads (parses a string). The s means string.

body_markdown:
## Why files and JSON matter

So far your programs forget everything when they stop. **Files** let your data survive — you save results, read inputs, and keep logs. And **JSON** is the standard way to store and exchange *structured* data: nearly every web API, config file, and AI tool speaks JSON.

As a maths graduate moving toward AI work, you'll meet JSON constantly — it's how you'll send prompts to models and read their replies.

## Reading and writing text files

Use `open()` with a **mode**, and always wrap it in a `with` block so the file closes automatically — even if something goes wrong.

```python
# Write a file (overwrites it)
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Hello, file!\n")
    f.write("Second line.\n")

# Read it back
with open("notes.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()
print(text)
```

## File modes

The mode string controls what you can do:

- `"r"` — read (the default); errors if the file is missing.
- `"w"` — write; **erases** the file first.
- `"a"` — append; adds to the end, keeping what's there.

Always pass `encoding="utf-8"` so accented characters never get mangled.

## What is JSON?

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is plain text that looks a lot like a Python dictionary: keys in quotes, values, and square brackets for lists. It's human-readable and understood by every language.

A JSON **object** becomes a Python **dict**; a JSON **array** becomes a **list**.

## Working with JSON in Python

The built-in `json` module converts between Python objects and JSON. Remember the **s = string** rule: `dumps`/`loads` use strings, `dump`/`load` use files.

```python
import json

user = {"name": "Dami", "skills": ["python", "git"], "hours": 30}

# Save to a file
with open("user.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(user, f, indent=2)

# Load it back into a Python dict
with open("user.json", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    data = json.load(f)

print(data["name"])        # Dami
print(data["skills"][0])   # python
```

## Your task

Save a small dictionary about yourself to a `profile.json` file, then write a second script that loads it and prints a friendly summary.

slides.title: Files & JSON
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month One. So far our programs forget everything the moment they stop running. In this lesson we fix that. You'll learn how to read and write files so your data survives, and then how to work with Jason, the format that powers almost every A P I and A I tool you'll ever touch. Let's dive in.

slides.title: Why files and JSON?
bullets: Files let your data outlive the program.
Save results, read inputs, keep logs.
JSON is how structured data travels.
Almost every API speaks JSON.
slides.narration: First, why does this matter? Right now your programs lose all their data when they end. Files change that, letting you save results, read inputs, and keep logs. And Jason is the standard way to move structured data around. Nearly every web A P I and A I tool sends and receives Jason, so this is a skill you'll use every single day.

slides.title: Opening a file
bullets: Use open() with a filename and a mode.
Wrap it in a with block.
with closes the file automatically.
Always pass encoding utf-8.
slides.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Hello, file!\n")
slides.narration: To work with a file we call open, giving it a filename and a mode. The golden rule is to wrap it in a with block. This guarantees the file closes safely when the block ends, even if an error happens. And always pass encoding equals utf eight, so accented characters are handled correctly on every system.

slides.title: Reading a file
bullets: Open in read mode with "r".
read() gives the whole file as text.
Loop over the file for line by line.
slides.code:
with open("notes.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()
print(text)
slides.narration: Reading is just as simple. We open the file in read mode, the letter r, and call read to get the entire contents back as one string. If a file is large, you can instead loop over it directly, which hands you one line at a time. Notice the text variable still works after the with block, because we read everything before the file closed.

slides.title: File modes
bullets: "r" reads (errors if missing).
"w" writes and erases first.
"a" appends to the end.
slides.code:
with open("log.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("new entry\n")
slides.narration: The mode you choose really matters. The letter r reads an existing file. The letter w writes, but be careful, it wipes the file clean before writing. And the letter a appends, adding to the end while keeping what's already there. For a log file you'll almost always want append mode, as shown here.

slides.title: What is JSON?
bullets: JSON is plain, readable text.
It looks like a Python dictionary.
Keys in quotes, values, lists in brackets.
Every language understands it.
slides.narration: So what is Jason? It stands for JavaScript Object Notation, but don't worry about the JavaScript part. It's simply plain text that looks remarkably like a Python dictionary. You get keys in quotes, their values, and square brackets for lists. It's easy for humans to read and understood by every programming language, which is exactly why the whole world settled on it.

slides.title: JSON maps to Python
bullets: A JSON object becomes a dict.
A JSON array becomes a list.
Strings, numbers, true/false, null map across.
So you work with familiar Python types.
slides.narration: Here's the friendly part. When you load Jason into Python, the pieces map onto types you already know. A Jason object becomes a dictionary. A Jason array becomes a list. Strings stay strings, numbers stay numbers, true and false become Python booleans, and null becomes None. So once it's loaded, you're just working with everyday Python.

slides.title: The json module
bullets: json.dump writes to a file.
json.load reads from a file.
dumps and loads use strings.
The s means string.
slides.code:
import json
user = {"name": "Dami", "hours": 30}
with open("user.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(user, f, indent=2)
slides.narration: Python's built in Jason module does the conversion for you. Use json dot dump to write a Python object straight into a file, and json dot load to read it back. There are also versions ending in s, dumps and loads, that work with strings instead of files. Just remember the s stands for string. The indent equals two argument here makes the saved file neatly formatted and easy to read.

slides.title: Loading JSON back
bullets: json.load returns a dict or list.
Access values like normal Python.
Round-trip: dump then load.
slides.code:
with open("user.json", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
print(data["name"])   # Dami
slides.narration: Loading Jason back is the reverse trip. We open the file in read mode and call json dot load, which hands us a normal Python dictionary. From there we access values exactly as we always have, using the keys. This dump then load cycle, saving data and reading it back, is the everyday workflow you'll use for config files, saved results, and A P I responses.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Using "w" and wiping a file by accident.
Forgetting encoding utf-8.
Mixing up dump and dumps.
Editing JSON by hand and breaking the syntax.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One, opening a file in write mode and accidentally erasing it, when you meant to append. Two, forgetting the encoding and corrupting special characters. Three, mixing up dump and dumps, remember the s is for strings. And four, hand editing a Jason file and breaking it with a missing comma or quote. Watch for these and you'll save yourself real headaches.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Files persist data; with closes them safely.
Modes: r reads, w overwrites, a appends.
JSON is text that maps to dicts and lists.
dump/load for files, dumps/loads for strings.
Task: save and reload a profile.json.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Files let your data survive, and the with statement closes them safely. The modes r, w, and a control reading, overwriting, and appending. Jason is readable text that maps cleanly onto Python dictionaries and lists, and the Jason module converts between them.
